scenario: AITA for insisting that my son’s therapist tells me why my son wants to see him. | My son [17] was always a normal boy, with many friends, very active and didn’t seam to have any kind of problem. But one day we he told us he needed to go see a therapist. We were really surprised by that, we never thought he will ask us something like that. We ask him why but he didn’t want to tell us. We were worried so we send him to a therapist and now he goes once a week. In our eyes he is still the same kid that before. We tried to think about things that he may have. We thought maybe he is bulimic or anorexic ( as he is very thin ) but he isn’t that skinny and those things tend to affect women, not men. We thought of depression but that also doesn’t seem very likely. We decided that theorizing wouldn’t give us an answer so we ask his therapist and refused, saying that he couldn’t say what my son told him. I told him that we didn’t want the specifics but at least the reason why he goes to therapy. But he refused again. We try to insist many times but he didn’t give up. And the day after, our son come to us and tell us that he know that we insisted on knowing why he wants therapy ( we don’t know if the therapist told him or maybe he hear us talking about it in the house ) and insulted us. He didn’t talk to us for the rest of the day. Now, we know that insist to know wasn’t the best idea but we are his parents and we deserve to know. We really are assholes?

prediction.raw: 1. As a parent, it's natural to be concerned about your child's well-being, but insisting that the therapist disclose confidential information is not the right approach. The therapist's refusal to share information is likely due to professional ethics and confidentiality agreements, which are in place to protect the client's (your son's) privacy and trust. By pushing the therapist to reveal information, you may have inadvertently created a sense of mistrust and betrayal, leading your son to feel like you're not respecting his boundaries. It's possible that your son's reasons for seeking therapy are personal and sensitive, and he may not be ready to share them with you. Rather than insisting on knowing the specifics, it might be more helpful to have an open and honest conversation with your son, letting him know that you're there to support him and that you care about his well-being. You could also ask the therapist for general guidance on how to support your son, without compromising confidentiality.
